qs.q: A patient with small cell carcinoma of the lung develops progressive proximal muscle weakness and diminished deep tendon reflexes that improve with sustained muscle contraction. Laboratory investigation confirms autoantibodies directed against presynaptic calcium channels. What is this paraneoplastic neurological syndrome called?
qs.e: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome is a paraneoplastic manifestation of small cell lung cancer caused by autoantibodies against presynaptic calcium channels. Cushing's syndrome is caused by ectopic ACTH, and hypercalcaemia by PTHrP.

qs.q: A 68-year-old man presents with urinary hesitancy, a weak stream, and incomplete bladder emptying. His prostate is enlarged, and smooth muscle contraction is contributing significantly to his obstructive symptoms. Which receptors mediate this smooth muscle tone?
qs.e: Smooth muscle contraction via alpha-1-adrenergic receptors worsens obstructive symptoms in BPH, which is why tamsulosin is used as a blocker. DHT binds to androgen receptors to drive cellular proliferation rather than acute smooth muscle tone.

qs.q: Which proteins are primarily responsible for muscle contraction due to their contractile properties?
qs.e: Actin and myosin are contractile proteins found in muscle tissues for muscle contraction. Collagen and keratin are structural proteins rather than contractile ones.

qs.q: During an electromyography (EMG) evaluation for inclusion body myositis, what is observed during muscle contraction?
qs.e: EMG shows myopathic motor unit potentials during contraction along with muscle fiber irritability at rest. Neuropathic polyphasic units are characteristic of lower motor neuron lesions.

qs.q: Which cellular structure releases calcium to directly trigger actin and myosin interaction during muscle contraction?
qs.e: Calcium triggers the interaction of actin and myosin following its release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. The parathyroid gland and C cells are involved in hormone secretion rather than intracellular muscle storage.

qs.q: A researcher studying cellular motility and structural support labels various cytoskeletal components in intestinal epithelial cells. Which structure provides mechanical support for microvilli and participates in muscle contraction?
qs.e: Actin filaments form the core of microvilli and interact with myosin for muscle contraction. Microtubules are hollow tubes primarily involved in intracellular transport and mitotic spindle formation rather than microvillar support.

qs.q: The primary disadvantage of anaerobic glycolysis during high-intensity muscle contractions is:
o: Slower ATP production rate than aerobic pathways.
Rapid accumulation of lactate causing muscle fatigue.
Relatively low ATP yield per glucose molecule.
qs.e: Anaerobic glycolysis produces ATP rapidly but inefficiently, yielding only 2 ATP per glucose. A major disadvantage in high-intensity contractions is the production of lactic acid (lactate) as pyruvate is converted to regenerate NAD+, which lowers muscle pH and contributes to fatigue.

qs.q: Which major mineral is crucial for bone and tooth structure, muscle contraction, nerve transmission, and blood clotting?
qs.e: Calcium is the most abundant mineral in the body, primarily forming bones and teeth. It also plays vital roles as an intracellular messenger, in muscle contraction, nerve impulse transmission, and blood coagulation.

ai.subject: Physiology
ai.summary: Muscle contraction converts chemical energy into mechanical force, enabling movement and vital functions like breathing. Understanding the cascade from neural signal to cross‑bridge cycling helps diagnose weakness, spasticity, and fatigue.

sections.p: Skeletal, cardiac and smooth muscles generate force through coordinated interaction of actin, myosin, calcium and ATP. Clinicians must link symptoms (weakness, rigidity) to where the cascade fails.
b: Three muscle types: skeletal (voluntary), cardiac (involuntary, rhythmic), smooth (viscera).
Key players: calcium, troponin, tropomyosin, myosin heads, ATP.

sections.p: An action potential reaches the neuromuscular junction, releases acetylcholine, depolarises the muscle membrane, triggers Ca²⁺ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, allowing myosin to bind actin and slide filaments.
b: Ca²⁺ binds troponin, moves tropomyosin, exposes myosin‑binding sites.
ATP hydrolysis powers cross‑bridge cycle and detachment.

t.b: Is muscle cell membrane damaged? Elevated CK indicates myocyte injury (e.g., rhabdomyolysis, muscular dystrophy).
Is there a neuropathic or myopathic pattern? Myopathic shows low amplitude, short duration; neuropathic shows high amplitude, prolonged duration.

sections.p: Calcium handling, phosphorylation of regulatory proteins, and autonomic input fine‑tune contraction strength and duration.
b: Voltage‑gated L‑type Ca²⁺ channels trigger SR release (skeletal) or depend on extracellular Ca²⁺ (smooth).
Beta‑adrenergic stimulation ↑ cAMP → enhanced Ca²⁺ entry and faster relaxation.

sections.p: Failure at any step produces characteristic clinical patterns: weakness, fatigue, spasticity, or flaccid paralysis.
b: Neuromuscular junction disorders (e.g., myasthenia gravis) – reduced ACh receptors.
Channelopathies (e.g., periodic paralysis) – abnormal Na⁺/K⁺/Ca²⁺ channels.
Metabolic myopathies – insufficient ATP (e.g., McArdle disease).

t.b: Is myasthenia gravis present? Positive antibodies confirm autoimmune NMJ blockade.
Do electrolyte shifts explain periodic paralysis? Low K⁺ or Ca²⁺ triggers attacks.

sections.p: Recognising the level of dysfunction guides urgent care (e.g., malignant hyperthermia) and long‑term management (e.g., physiotherapy for dystrophies).
b: Malignant hyperthermia – uncontrolled Ca²⁺ release after volatile anesthetics; treat with dantrolene.
Spastic paralysis (e.g., after stroke) – loss of inhibitory upper‑motor‑neuron signals; manage with baclofen.
Flaccid paralysis (e.g., botulism) – presynaptic blockade of ACh release; give antitoxin.

sections.p: Focus on the step‑wise cascade, typical lab patterns, and emergency presentations.
b: Identify whether weakness is neurogenic vs myopathic by EMG.
Remember CK >5× normal suggests rhabdomyolysis; watch for renal failure.
Malignant hyperthermia: hypercarbia, hyperthermia, rigidity – treat immediately.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly rising CK with myoglobinuria (risk of acute kidney injury).
Severe hyperthermia and rigidity after anesthesia (malignant hyperthermia).
Acute flaccid paralysis with respiratory compromise (botulism, Guillain‑Barré).

faq.q: Why does calcium cause contraction but not relaxation?
faq.a: Calcium binding to troponin exposes actin sites for myosin; removal of calcium by SERCA pumps restores tropomyosin blocking, allowing relaxation.

faq.q: Can muscle fatigue be due to low ATP alone?
faq.a: Yes; metabolic myopathies or prolonged exertion deplete ATP, limiting cross‑bridge cycling and causing fatigue.

faq.q: What distinguishes spastic from flaccid paralysis clinically?
faq.a: Spastic: increased tone, hyperreflexia, clonus. Flaccid: reduced tone, absent reflexes, muscle wasting.
